item.title: European stocks close higher. Spain leads while the dollar strengthens
item.description:
As London and European traders head home, the major European stock indices have closed higher across the board. Spain’s Ibex led the gains with a rise of 1.33%, followed by the UK’s FTSE 100, up nearly 1%.

item.title: The broader indices are all lower with the Nasdaq 100 the weakest. What are the technicals tell traders right now?
item.description:

Recall that all three closed at record levels last Tuesday before retreating on Wednesday and Thursday. Friday’s rebound improved the technical picture, but today’s declines are taking some of that bullish momentum away.

The key reference remains the rising 100-hour moving average. Last week’s lows held at or near that moving average for each index, giving buyers a level to lean against and keeping them in control.

Today, however, the technical stories are starting to diverge:

  • S&P: The 100-hour moving average is at 7738.18. Today’s low reached 7802.58, with the index currently at 7809.96. Buyers remain in control above the moving average.

  • NASDAQ Composite: The 100-hour moving average is at 27151.12. Today’s low reached 27240.47, with the index currently near 27275. The bullish bias remains intact, but the cushion above support is smaller.

  • NASDAQ 100: The 100-hour moving average is at 30689.21. Today’s low extended below that level to 30633.80, giving sellers a modest technical advantage. Staying below the moving average would keep sellers more in control in the short term. Moving back above it would weaken that bearish signal.

For traders, the lesson is straightforward: a down day does not automatically change the technical bias. Where the price trades relative to support matters. The S&P and NASDAQ Composite are still holding above their key moving averages. The NASDAQ 100 has breached its support, and sellers now need to keep the price below it.

item.title: Gold falls toward hourly moving averages. Can sellers keep control?
item.description:
Gold has rotated lower after reaching a session high of $4,217.19, falling short of the October 2 high at $4,226.83. The price subsequently fell to $4,154.79 and is currently trading near $4,167, down $27.50, or 0.65%.

Reports that Kazakhstan has begun selling gold are attracting attention, while the higher Treasury-yield backdrop is also being cited as a headwind. Ironically, the US treasury market is closed today for the Columbus Day holiday. So although yields are higher, blaming it on higher yields today is kind of a stretch.

Nevertheless, gold pays no interest. When Treasury yields rise, investors can earn more from holding government debt, increasing the opportunity cost of holding gold. That can weigh on demand, although the relationship does not work perfectly every day.

Put the Kazakhstan headline in perspective

The World Gold Council’s September report showed that gold accounted for approximately 75% of Kazakhstan’s reserves. It also showed that the country had accumulated 29 tonnes through July. With that much of its reserves concentrated in gold, some diversification would be understandable. That is a possible explanation, rather than confirmation of the reason for any current sales.

One country selling does not establish a broader central-bank selling trend. The size, timing and purpose of the sales matter.

My take? The headline is another ingredient in the pot that determines price. It may contribute to short-term selling, but I would hesitate to call it a game changer by itself.

The headline gets attention. The technicals define the next test.

Today’s high fell short of the October high. Buyers had their shot at extending toward that level, but could not get there before the price rotated lower. That gives sellers an initial victory.

The decline has now brought two important technical levels into play:

  • 200-hour moving average: $4,167.60

  • 100-hour moving average: $4,152.92

At a price near $4,167, gold is just below the 200-hour moving average but remains above the 100-hour moving average. Today’s low at $4,154.79 also held just above that lower moving average.

That distinction matters. Sellers have made progress, but they have more work to do.

Moving averages give traders reference points for judging control and defining risk. They do not guarantee that support will hold. The useful information comes from how the price behaves around them.

What would strengthen the bearish case?

For sellers, staying below the 200-hour moving average would keep the immediate pressure on. The next step would be a break below the 100-hour moving average at $4,152.92.

Getting below both—and staying below—would tilt the technical bias more to the downside.

A brief dip below support followed by a quick recovery would be less convincing. Traders should watch for follow-through: can the price remain below the broken level, and do rebounds find sellers against it?

What would give buyers another opportunity?

For buyers, the first job is to defend the 100-hour moving average. The next is to reclaim the 200-hour moving average at $4,167.60 and stay above it.

That would suggest the selling pressure is easing and give buyers a chance to rotate back toward today’s high at $4,217.19, followed by the October high at $4,226.83.

Holding support is a start. Reclaiming the higher moving average would strengthen the buyers’ case.

Holidays deserve a different lens

Today is a U.S. bond-market holiday in observance of Columbus Day.

Holiday participation can be thinner, allowing a headline to produce a larger price reaction than it might during a busier session. That is a possibility, not proof that today’s move is exaggerated.

For traders, the lesson is to respect the headline while watching whether the market can sustain the move through a meaningful technical level.

The news can provide the shove and that shove may be exaggerated today. The technicals help us judge whether buyers or sellers are taking control—and give us a level against which to define and limit risk.

For gold, the next battle is clear: $4,152.92 below and $4,167.60 above. Watch which side the price breaks, whether it stays there, and whether momentum follows.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin buyers had their shot above the 200-hour MA. They missed.
item.description:
Bitcoin is trading near its session low at $82,389 after reaching a high of $84,254 earlier today.

That high took the price above the 200-hour moving average (green line), currently at $83,877. The break gave buyers an opportunity to build upside momentum. Instead, the move failed, buyers turned to sellers, and the price rotated lower.

The decline has since taken bitcoin below its 100-hour moving average at $82,786, giving sellers another short-term technical victory.

Can they keep the pressure on?

24 days of range trading

Looking at the bigger picture, bitcoin has spent the last 24 days—since September 18—trading between $80,106 and $87,374. There has been plenty of up-and-down price action, but no sustained break from that range.

Last Tuesday, buyers made another run toward the upper extreme but stalled ahead of the target. The subsequent reversal took the price below both the 100- and 200-hour moving averages.

Apart from brief breaks above the 200-hour moving average on Sunday and again today, the price has remained below that indicator, keeping the technical bias more bearish.

What sellers need to do next

On the downside, the price is now within a swing area between $81,183 and $82,653. Sellers need to push below the lower boundary at $81,183 to open the door for a test of $80,106—the September 20 low that was revisited last week.

Break below $80,106 and stay below, and sellers would finally have a move outside the broader trading range, opening the door for further downside momentum.

Until then, support still needs to be broken. Sellers have more work to do.

What buyers need to reclaim

For buyers, the first step is to reclaim the 100-hour moving average at $82,786. Above that, the 200-hour moving average at $83,877 remains the key hurdle. Getting above and staying above that level would give buyers another opportunity to take back control.

The buyers had their shot today. They missed. Sellers have the advantage below the hourly moving averages, but they still need to break support to turn that advantage into a bigger move lower.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: EUR/USD consolidates at the lows as France's budget and US CPI remain in focus
item.description:
The US dollar has been supported recently despite a dovish repricing triggered by Fed’s Williams and Fed’s Jefferson comments that pushed back against expectations of a rate hike in October.

The main reason were risk-off flows into the greenback due to European debt concerns. The focus has been particularly on France, where political uncertainty and concerns over the country's large fiscal deficit have recently pushed French government bond yields higher and widened the spread over German Bunds to its highest level since the eurozone debt crisis.

A stabilization in French spreads could allow some of the euro's risk premium to unwind and trigger a pullback in the US dollar, while further widening and contagion to other countries would likely keep the greenback supported.

Moreover, the US-Iran negotiations continue to be at a stalemate but at least Trump ruled out new strikes before the November elections last week. This week, we also have the US CPI report on the agenda, which could trigger big moves in the markets.

A hotter than expected core CPI could bring a rate hike in October back on the table and give the US dollar a boost. A soft report, on the other hand, will likely weigh on the greenback in the short-term on a fall in Treasury yields.

On the EUR side, the probabilities of an ECB rate hike in October have faded following the sharp widening in the French-German bond spread, as policymakers are likely to remain cautious about adding further pressure to already fragile financial markets.

However, markets still expect the ECB to raise rates in December, reflecting persistent inflationary pressures due to higher energy prices. In terms of economic data, the latest Eurozone CPI showed headline inflation surging to 3.8% in September from 3.2% in August, largely due to higher energy prices. Core inflation remained relatively contained, edging up to 2.5% from 2.4%.

Looking ahead, energy prices and developments in the Middle East will remain important drivers of the inflation outlook. Any sustained decline in energy prices could reduce near-term inflation pressure and give the ECB more room to delay further tightening. This would also be positive for the euro on improved risk sentiment and lower Fed rate hike expectations.

The euro will also remain sensitive to developments in the bond market, particularly the French-German spread. France’s government has proposed a 2027 budget targeting a deficit of 5.0% of GDP, supported by spending restraint and higher tax revenues. This is lower than the previously 5.4% and helped ease market concerns somewhat. However, the plan still faces parliamentary hurdles, and Eurozone finance ministers and the ECB have urged France to pass a credible budget to restore market confidence.

Traders will keep a close eye on France where improvements would be positive for the euro, while negative outcomes will likely continue to weigh on the single currency.

 

EURUSD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that EURUSDhas been selling off heavily in the past weeks on France’s debt woes. The nearest key support is around the 1.1067 level. If the price gets there, we can expect the buyers to step in, with a defined risk below the level, to position for a recovery into the major downward trendline. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to increase the bearish bets into the 1.08 handle next.

EURUSD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we have a downward trendline defining the selloff since early September. The sellers will likely continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep pushing into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break to start positioning into the major downward trendline, with the 1.1285 level as the first target.

EURUSD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we can see that the pair has been bottoming out since the French proposed budget deficit for 2027 got lowered to 5.0% from 5.4%. We have a support zone around the 1.1160 level. The buyers will likely continue to step in around the support, with a defined risk below it, to keep targeting a break above the trendline and new highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to increase the bearish bets into new lows. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

On Wednesday we have the US CPI report. On Thursday, we get the US PPI, the US Retail Sales and the latest US Jobless Claims figures. 

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive European session wrap: Oil rebounds, dollar firms as US bond market holiday keeps traders cautious
item.description:

  • European equities higher; S&P 500 futures +0.1%

It was a quieter session in European morning trade today as broader markets have to contend with a US partial market holiday to start the new week.

The US bond market is closed in observance of Columbus day and while the stock market remains open, traders and investors are still missing one key piece of the puzzle in broader markets today. That is especially the case since surging Treasury yields have been a major driver of trading sentiment over the past few weeks.

As such, the absence of a key signal for broader markets is providing some room for a bit of a breather. But at the same time, thinner liquidity conditions could also lead to some exacerbated price moves as we get things going in the new week.

Oil prices were down early on but recovered well to be up over 1% on the day currently. Hopes of a Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire helped to drag prices down in the early stages before the focus turned back towards tensions in the Middle East, where supply disruptions continue to weigh on the market mood. WTI crude was down to just under $90 earlier in the day but is trading back up to near $93 currently.

Meanwhile, the dollar is holding slightly firmer as it posts a light advance against the rest of the major currencies bloc. USD/JPY is up 0.2% to 158.60 while EUR/USD is down 0.2% to 1.1175, so the gains are not anything to shout about for the time being.

As for equities, European stocks are enjoying a modest start after a rough period in trading last week. While regional bond yields are still keeping the pressure on, investors are able to take some comfort from the broader market mood - at least for now. Looking to US futures, it's a bit more of a mixed mood with tech shares sagging a little ahead of the open later. S&P 500 futures are up 0.1% while Nasdaq futures are down 0.2% so far on the day.

And in the commodities space, gold is also down 0.5% to $4,170 after another technical rejection from the $4,200-20 region once again.

Until the bond market returns tomorrow, I wouldn't read too much into the market moves today. Thinner liquidity conditions could exaggerate price movements in the session ahead, making it harder to judge whether any of the moves have genuine conviction behind them.

The first thing to watch now will be how Treasury yields respond when trading resumes tomorrow. That should offer a better indication of whether the calmer mood today has any staying power, especially with inflation pressures and the Fed outlook still hanging over markets.

After which, the focus will quickly turn to the US CPI report on Wednesday to dictate how things might play out for the remainder of the week.

item.title: SpaceX telecom selloff: TMUS, T, VZ rebound? Plus CCC and IREN
item.description:
SpaceX sent telecom stocks plunging. Is Monday's premarket bounce a buying opportunity or a trap?

Monday, October 12, 2026 | U.S. premarket stock movers | Prices delayed approximately 15 minutes

T-Mobile, AT&T and Verizon suffered heavy losses on Friday after SpaceX unveiled a spectrum acquisition that could eventually challenge traditional mobile networks. Monday's early premarket trading shows a modest recovery, but the damage is largely intact. Meanwhile, telecom tower operators have retained most of their remarkable gains. Are investors correctly pricing a competitive revolution, or getting ahead of the evidence?

As also navigate this week's tricky market structure, I'm closely watching the shifting liquidity dynamics because the Nasdaq could be vulnerable to near-term weakness as options traders aggressively hedge into the upcoming US CPI release.

With the index fighting to defend critical VWAP levels, this macroeconomic uncertainty is colliding directly with a massive fundamental catalyst.

My primary focus on the tape right now is whether TSMC can keep the broader AI boom running while that same inflation print looms over the tech sector's valuation multiples.

If you are actively managing risk around these institutional flows, it's essential to understand why the first major companies to report are so critical to watch, as their initial order flow and forward guidance will ultimately dictate the directional bias and implied volatility for the rest of the quarter.

Why did SpaceX send telecom stocks plunging?

SpaceX has agreed to acquire Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz spectrum portfolio, subject to Federal Communications Commission approval and other closing conditions.

The agreement, announced on October 8, is an important development for SpaceX's Starlink Mobile ambitions.

Low-band spectrum is particularly valuable because its signals travel relatively long distances and penetrate buildings more effectively than higher-frequency signals. This could help SpaceX combine satellite connectivity with ground-based mobile infrastructure.

In other words, SpaceX is taking steps toward becoming a more formidable competitor to established wireless operators.

Investors responded forcefully on Friday, October 9.

Traditional mobile carriers were punished as investors reassessed future competition. Tower infrastructure companies rallied as investors anticipated that SpaceX might need their infrastructure to build out its terrestrial network.

But there is an important distinction between what the market expects and what has actually happened.

SpaceX has announced a spectrum acquisition, not the immediate displacement of established mobile carriers.

And while tower operators could benefit from an additional customer investing in network deployment, prospective demand is not yet confirmed leasing revenue.

The market may therefore be pricing two developments simultaneously: potentially weaker economics for existing carriers and potentially stronger economics for tower operators.

Both outcomes remain uncertain.

Monday's bounce: How much of Friday's damage has actually been repaired?

Early Monday trading offers a useful reality check.

The early market has modestly extended Friday's gains, although this is not confirmation of sustained buying.

Snapshot for today's premarket? Delayed early premarket quotes; limited liquidity.

The most interesting observation is not simply that the carriers are somewhat bouncing.

It is that the market's original relative preference for tower companies over mobile carriers remains largely unchanged.

That provides a useful comparison for the regular session.

If carriers begin recovering meaningfully while tower shares give back their gains, investors may be reconsidering the magnitude or timing of the original competitive assumptions.

If the divergence persists, the market may still be assigning substantial value to SpaceX's longer-term ambitions.

Neither outcome proves that the underlying market assessment is correct.

Could this become a contrarian opportunity?

Possibly. But a lower price does not automatically mean a stock has become undervalued.

Consider two competing interpretations.

The case that Friday's telecom selloff was excessive

SpaceX may ultimately become a serious competitor, but building a nationwide service capable of challenging established operators requires regulatory approvals, capital investment, infrastructure, customer acquisition and time.

Meanwhile, incumbent operators retain existing customers, established networks and ongoing service revenues. Their businesses do not disappear because a potential competitor acquires spectrum.

If investors have priced years of competitive pressure into a single trading session, some of Friday's selling could eventually prove excessive.

The case that investors are identifying a genuine long-term threat

SpaceX is not merely announcing an idea. Its spectrum transaction is a concrete strategic commitment.

The company could potentially change how mobile connectivity is delivered, especially in areas underserved by conventional networks.

Even before substantial customer losses occur, an increasingly credible competitor could influence future pricing, investment requirements and expected profit margins.

That matters to valuation today, because investors value companies partly on the earnings they expect them to produce years into the future.

The key question is therefore not whether SpaceX has already damaged telecom earnings.

It is how much future competitive damage the market has already priced in, and whether that assessment will ultimately prove reasonable.

The same logic applies in reverse to tower operators. Potential future network demand deserves attention, but it should not be confused with contracts already signed or revenue already secured.

Telecom stock levels worth watching on Monday

The following levels are reference points from Friday's regular session, not automatic trading signals.

T-Mobile: $147.90 support reference, $148.58 Friday close

A sustained recovery above $148.58 during more liquid trading would be an initial indication that buyers are stabilizing the stock. Renewed weakness below $147.90 would suggest that selling pressure remains unresolved.

AT&T: $21.96 support reference, $22.18 Friday close

The early recovery is negligible. Traders can watch whether AT&T attracts sustained demand above Friday's close or revisits its low, while accounting for the dividend adjustment when comparing performance.

Verizon: $40.81 support reference, $41.65 Friday close

Verizon's close is an initial recovery reference. A sustained advance above it would be more constructive than an isolated premarket uptick, while a move below $40.81 would weaken the stabilization case.

Crown Castle: $79.64 Friday close

Holding near Friday's closing price would suggest that investors continue to assign value to potential infrastructure demand. A substantial reversal would invite closer examination of whether expectations advanced too quickly.

American Tower: $182.24 Friday close

The same principle applies. Holding its gains supports the initial market reaction, but a significant giveback could indicate that investors are reassessing the timing and scale of potential benefits.

These reference levels should be evaluated alongside trading volume, liquidity and the broader market. A brief price move through a level is not necessarily evidence of sustained acceptance.

Two more U.S. stock movers worth watching

CCC Intelligent Solutions: A takeover premium without a confirmed takeover price

CCC Intelligent Solutions (CCC), which provides software used in the automotive insurance industry, gained 6.85% on Friday to close at $7.02.

Its early Monday premarket indication was approximately $7.60, another 8.26% higher.

Bloomberg reported that private equity firm GTCR and Elliott Investment Management were in advanced discussions to acquire the company. However, a final agreement had not been reached, and the negotiations could still change or collapse.

This makes CCC particularly interesting from an educational perspective.

When a company announces a definitive cash takeover agreement, investors can compare its share price with the agreed consideration. The difference, often called the merger-arbitrage spread, reflects factors including deal-completion risk and the time required to close.

But CCC is not at that stage.

There is no confirmed acquisition price against which to calculate a dependable spread.

The stock is therefore responding to expectations about a possible transaction, not a guaranteed payout.

What to watch:Whether the premarket rally survives more liquid trading, and whether definitive terms are announced. If talks fail, a portion of the speculative takeover premium could disappear quickly.

IREN: An AI customer report raises a different valuation question

IREN (IREN), the Bitcoin-mining and AI infrastructure company, declined 1.46% on Friday to $35.19.

Monday's early premarket indication was approximately $37.06, up 5.32% from Friday's close.

However, investors should distinguish four things:

  • Contracted capacity:Computing infrastructure a customer has agreed to use.

  • Recognized revenue:Revenue recorded as services are delivered under the applicable accounting rules.

  • Operating profitability:The earnings remaining after the relevant operating expenses.

  • Free cash flow:Cash remaining after operating cash needs and capital expenditures.

A commercially attractive customer relationship can still require substantial financing and infrastructure spending before it produces meaningful free cash flow.

A promising recovery can be interrupted by broader selling, just as a weak stock can be lifted temporarily by a rising market.

The telecom sector is responding to a potential structural change in competition.

IREN is responding to reported customer information that could strengthen future AI infrastructure economics, without yet establishing the resulting profitability.

Sometimes the market gets ahead of reality. Sometimes it correctly anticipates a change long before the financial statements reveal it. The task for traders and investors is to distinguish between those possibilities, without assuming that the first bounce provides the answer.

item.title: Why winning more trades doesn't always make you a profitable trader
item.description:
If someone walks up to you and says that they have more winning trades than they do losing ones, you would think that they are probably making bank. I mean, it sounds perfectly logical, no? If you're getting most of your trades right, then it makes sense that you should be making money.

But what if I told you that winning more trades doesn't necessarily mean that you would be making money? It sounds convoluted now but that's where understanding your win rate and how that ties to risk/reward becomes important.

If you're winning more than you are losing, that means you should have a win rate of over 50% in your trades. It can be something like 60% or maybe even higher like 80%. However, a high win rate doesn't automatically mean that you're going to be a profitable trader. The more important part of the equation to consider is arguably how much money are you actually making when you win compared to how much money are you losing when the trade goes bad.

To make things easier to understand, let's go back to the apple store example again from our previous educational posts (yes, I love my apples).

Just imagine you are buying apples from a supplier and then selling them to customers, hoping to make a tidy profit along the way. And let's say out of every 10 apple sales, you manage to make money on 6 of them. That's a win rate of 60%. Sounds decent enough, no? But here's the catch.

Suppose you make $3 in profit on each successful apple sale. But during times when business is poor and for some reason you're forced to sell the apples at a discount, you end up losing $6 instead. After 10 apple sales, here is how the numbers add up:

  • 6 profitable sales at $3 each = $18 in profits
  • 4 losing sales at $6 each = $24 in losses
  • Overall sales = $6 loss

Ouch. You're getting things right more often than you do wrong, but yet you still end up losing money. That's not the way to run a successful business now is it? So, what exactly was the problem?

From a trading perspective, this is where the concept of risk/reward ratio comes into play. To put things more simply, it is how you handle the approach of measuring how much money that you are risking on a trade compared to how much that you are hoping to make.

Going back to the apple store example, you are essentially risking $6 to make just $3. That is a risk/reward ratio of just 1:0.5. But what if we flipped those numbers around instead?

Let's say you are still making money from 6 out of every 10 apple sales, but this time you are making $6 on a good sale and only losing $3 on a bad sale. Now, this is how those numbers would look like after another 10 apple sales:

  • 6 profitable sales at $6 each = $36 in profits
  • 4 losing sales at $3 each = $12 in losses
  • Overall sales = $24 profit

It's the same win rate but the outcome is entirely different.

Now of course, actual trading in itself is not that straightforward. There are so many other things to consider, besides the fact that you also can't just simply decide to make bigger profits and take smaller losses every time. Markets don't always play out to how we think they might and that can change our trading conviction as well as where we place our stops and profit targets.

But if there's one lesson to be learned here, it is that the more important thing isn't necessarily about trying to win as many trades as possible. Finding the right balance between your win rate and how much you're actually making or losing on each trade is arguably even more crucial to a trader.

Let's be real. I'd much rather have a lower win rate but stay profitable than wanting to be right more often, only to have my losing trades wipe out all my money.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

OPEC has just announced a rather significant downgrade to its oil demand outlook for this year. The bloc slashed its growth forecast to just 400,000 bpd, down from the 1.4 million bpd it had projected at the start of the year. Now, that's quite a substantial revision to say the least.

According to OPEC secretary general, Haitham Al Ghais, the latest downgrade reflects the developments in the oil market throughout the year. And they are also still expecting some of that deferred demand to materialise some time in 2027. In other words, OPEC is anticipating that there will be a recovery in consumption conditions next year.

Having said that, the present outlook is arguably the more pressing issue for oil traders. Despite the weaker demand outlook, prices are still keeping elevated with Brent crude seen above $105 and WTI crude trading back above $92 today. That's largely due to the ongoing tensions in the Middle East, which are continuing to keep supply risks firmly in the picture.

The latest attacks on oil tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthi strike on Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport over the weekend serve as a timely reminder that tensions are still running high. And that means the oil market will have to be cautious as disruptions to shipping flows could worsen further at any time.

It's one thing to have less demand for oil but it is a whole other thing when supply is still struggling to get to where it needs to go.

So until we do see a material improvement to the developments in the Middle East, it will be tough to take OPEC's latest downgrade and use that as a reason to form a more bearish view on oil prices. Sure, the demand outlook may be weakening. However, supply risks are still calling the shots for now.

item.title: Connecting the dots: Following the money behind the AI boom on Wall Street
item.description:
Just about everyone wants a piece of the AI pie these days. Tech companies are spending big and investors are dreaming even bigger. It seems like nobody wants to miss out.

With billions of dollars being poured into AI, there is a lot of money to go around and also to be made - or at least that is what everyone is hoping for at the end of the day. But the main question remains, where exactly is all this money going?

For the most part, you have your big tech giants spending heavily on building data centers and buying up powerful chips in order to run their respective AI services.

And that means the companies that are supplying all this equipment are among the first to benefit from the spending boom. Yup, those are the likes of Nvidia and TSMC for example. The former designs advanced chips while the latter manufactures them. And so the more money that is being spent on AI infrastructure, the greater the potential demand for their products and services. In turn, that potentially translates to higher sales and bigger profits - which investors will look to bet on in the stock market.

I would say that is arguably the more straightforward part. The other part is one that is more tricky to navigate as it doesn't just involve how much money that all of these companies are making today. It's about pricing in how much they could potentially earn in the years ahead.

We've been seeing this story run for the better part of three years now, with investors willing to pay higher valuations amid expectations of continued AI spending to drive even higher future profits. But therein lies the catch, much of the enthusiasm and excitement is based on expectations of future growth.

But what happens if AI spending starts slowing down? Or perhaps the companies that are spending all these billions eventually find that they're not making enough money from AI services to justify their investments? The latter in particular has been a question that has been challenging the Wall Street narrative for more than a year already, but is yet to really do much damage to the rally in tech stocks.

Nonetheless, growing concerns if left unchecked could quickly change up the mood on Wall Street. I mean, even strong earnings might not be enough to keep stock prices going higher if investors continue to keep pricing in something much better.

In that regard, TSMC's earnings later this week will be another useful checkpoint for investors. That is especially the case with elevated Treasury yields already making lofty technology stock valuations harder and harder to justify.

There's certainly no shortage of money chasing the AI boom but as much as everyone wants a piece of the pie, it will depend a lot on whether all this spending can deliver the profits to match.

item.title: What is earnings season and why the first companies to report are important to watch
item.description:
Four times a year, publicly traded companies release their financial results, giving investors a picture of how businesses are performing, whether conditions are improving or deteriorating, and whether current stock prices are justified by future profit expectations.

For investors, earnings are about comparing actual results with expectations, assessing what management expects in the coming quarters, and determining whether the new information changes the outlook for future earnings.

What is earnings season?

Earnings season is a specific multi-week period each quarter when a vast majority of publicly traded companies cluster together to release their official financial earning (revenue, profits, and losses) and reports for the previous quarter. In the United States, it typically takes place four times a year, following the end of each fiscal quarter.

The main reporting periods generally fall in January and February, April and May, July and August, and October and November. The exact timing varies by company because businesses have different fiscal calendars and reporting deadlines.

During these periods, companies publish their quarterly earnings reports, which usually include an income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement, comparisons with previous periods, and management commentary. Many companies also hold earnings calls, where executives explain the results and answer questions from analysts and investors.

Earnings season attracts considerable attention because it provides a concentrated flow of new information about corporate profitability. Instead of receiving information about individual companies gradually throughout the quarter, investors receive results from hundreds of businesses over a relatively short period.

Image: Earnings Calendar for the current week on earningswhispers.com

In what order do companies report earnings?

There is no official order in which companies must report their results. Each company announces its own reporting date, subject to applicable disclosure rules and its fiscal calendar. Nevertheless, earnings season tends to follow a recognizable pattern.

Large US banks often report near the beginning of the season. JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citigroup and Goldman Sachs are frequently among the early major reporters. Their results are followed by companies from other industries, including technology, industrials, consumer goods, healthcare and energy.

Large technology companies, such as Microsoft, Apple, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta, often report later in the season, although the exact order varies from quarter to quarter.

The first companies to report can also provide investors with an early indication of the economic conditions affecting their industries. Banks, for example, offer information about loan demand, credit quality, consumer finances, corporate borrowing and investment banking activity. Technology companies provide clues about business spending, cloud demand, advertising markets and investment in artificial intelligence. Retailers offer insight into consumer spending, pricing power and inventory conditions. 

Why can the first company to report move an entire sector?

The stock market is forward-looking. Investors do not value a company solely on its current profits. They estimate how much money it will generate in the future and discount those expected cash flows back to the present. This means that information about one company can influence the valuation of other companies exposed to similar economic conditions.

Imagine that a major US bank reports stronger than expected loan growth, resilient net interest income and lower than anticipated credit losses. Investors may conclude that the banking sector is benefiting from healthier borrowers and more favourable lending conditions. They could then raise their earnings expectations for other banks, even before those companies publish their own results, leading to a rise in stock prices.

The opposite can happen if a company reports deteriorating demand, rising costs or weaker guidance. Investors may assume that other businesses facing similar conditions could experience the same problems. 

Companies in the same sector share common economic drivers. Banks are sensitive to interest rates, credit conditions and loan demand. Semiconductor companies are exposed to chip demand, capital expenditure and inventory cycles. Retailers depend on consumer spending, wages and pricing power. Information from one company can therefore reveal something about the environment facing its competitors.

Moreover, many investment funds trade entire sectors through exchange-traded funds, baskets of stocks and sector-specific strategies. A change in the perceived outlook for an industry can therefore generate buying or selling across several companies at once.

Keep in mind, though, that the reaction is not always uniform. A company may benefit from market-share gains at the expense of competitors, or it may have company-specific problems that do not affect the rest of the sector. Investors need to distinguish between information that reflects a broad industry trend from information unique to the reporting company.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Market playbook: What if US CPI comes in hot but stocks refuse to fall?
item.description:
The main focus in markets this week will be on the US CPI report due Wednesday, 14 October. The inflation numbers for September will be heavily scrutinised as traders and investors are very much still caught in trying to weigh the inflation outlook as well as risks of the Fed raising interest rates further. And all of that is made even more crucial as Treasury yields are threatening multi-decade highs in the past week or so.

The usual expectation is that a hotter-than-expected inflation report will be bad news for stocks. But what if we actually get that but Wall Street refuses to play ball and stocks do not happen to fall? That is a rather interesting scenario, no?

To start, let's just consider what the typical market reaction should be. Higher inflation would mean that the Fed might have to keep interest rates "higher for longer" or even raise them further to deal with stronger price pressures in general.

As things stand, Fed funds futures are currently pricing in roughly an 81% probability that the Fed will keep interest rates unchanged later this month. As such, a hotter-than-expected inflation report could challenge that pricing expectations and see traders push for bets on another rate hike. If not, it could at least reinforce expectations of another move in December.

In turn, that rightfully should translate to higher Treasury yields and a stronger dollar. And for stocks, that's usually not a good combination to deal with. Higher yields make borrowing more expensive for companies while also making bonds more attractive relative to equities. In turn, that could put downward pressure on stock valuations, particularly among big tech.

However, what happens if the market reaction isn't what we expect it to be and stocks don't move according to how they should? How should we approach that as a trader?

Well, the first is to understand what might be causing such a market reaction. Perhaps it is a case that traders had already positioned themselves for a hot inflation reading, meaning much of the bad news was priced in beforehand. Or it could be a case of the devil being in the details, with the headline number looking ugly but the underlying inflation details aren't quite as worrying.

Having said that, I'd still be wary of immediately treating that resilience as a bullish signal. The thing I want to see is whether stocks can build on the initial reaction, especially if Treasury yields continue climbing. Sure, stocks might hold firmer in the first 15 to 30 minutes after the data. But if yields keep pushing higher and equities start losing ground a couple of hours later, then perhaps that initial resilience wasn't quite as convincing as it first appeared.

Besides that, it will also be worth watching whether the buying in the stock market is more broad-based or merely supported by a handful of big tech names. That will provide some idea of what is actually carrying the market mood in equities should there be contradicting signals from the likes of bonds and the dollar.

So, don't just focus and trade on the headline numbers from the US CPI report. It would be wise to also pay attention to how markets react in the hours that follow as the absence of a selloff can arguably tell us more than the inflation numbers themselves.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold futures swing trade idea: Four buy entries and four upside targets

Gold futures swing trade idea: A patient buy ladder with four upside targets

Gold futures (GC/MGC) | October 12, 2026 | Multi-week swing trade

Gold futures are trading near $4,215 in the supplied October 12 snapshot, following a substantial correction from the late-August highs near $4,755. Although a bullish reversal is not yet confirmed, buyers appear to be defending the broader $4,100 to $4,160 region. My preferred approach is to wait for lower prices and build a position gradually, rather than chase the recovery.

The strategy involves four potential buy entries, a defined protective stop and four profit targets. Larger allocations are reserved for deeper pullbacks, but some orders may never execute.

Swing trade at a glance

Weighted-average entry: $4,172.98Assumes all four orders fill.Protective stop: $4,126.60Trade exit level, not proof that the wider support region has failed.Blended reward-to-risk: 4.27:13 / 3 / 3 / 1 target allocation.Planned gross risk: $4,638Ten Micro Gold contracts; excludes commissions, slippage and gaps.

Building the position: Four buy orders

Rather than entering the full position near $4,215, the proposed strategy distributes 10 Micro Gold futures contracts (MGC) across four lower prices. Together, they equal the exposure of one standard GC contract. The bars show each order’s share of the full position, not a forecast for gold prices.

Buy 1 | $4,198.60   1 micro contract (10%)Buy 2 | $4,194.50   2 micro contracts (20%)Buy 3 | $4,169.80   3 micro contracts (30%)Buy 4 | $4,158.20   4 micro contracts (40%)Full-position weighted-average entry: $4,172.98

A shallow correction creates only limited exposure, while a deeper pullback allows a larger position at more favorable prices. But a lower average does not automatically make a trade safer. Falling prices can also indicate that sellers are getting stronger. Gold could instead rebound without reaching the lower orders, leaving a smaller position with a different average entry and risk profile.

Four upside targets for a possible gold recovery

Profit targets and reward-to-risk

TP1: $4,257 | 1.81:1An initial recovery objective and opportunity to consider partial profits.TP2: $4,338 | 3.56:1A more meaningful repair of the bearish structure.TP3: $4,425 | 5.43:1A stronger recovery supporting improving bullish momentum.TP4, runner: $4,648 | 10.24:1An ambitious move toward the region of the preceding highs.

These reward-to-risk ratios assume all ten entries are filled and use the resulting weighted-average entry. An equal 25% allocation to the four targets would produce approximately 5.26:1. But ten contracts cannot be split evenly across four targets in whole contracts. A practical alternative is to exit three at TP1, three at TP2, three at TP3 and one at TP4. That yields a blended 4.27:1.

Potential gross profit by target

The following bar comparison illustrates profit contributions for the 3 / 3 / 3 / 1 exits if all entry orders fill and every exit order executes as planned. Amounts are in U.S. dollars and exclude transaction costs.

TP1 (3 contracts): $2,520.60TP2 (3 contracts): $4,950.60TP3 (3 contracts): $7,560.60TP4 (1 contract): $4,750.20

Illustrative financial outcomes

Potential total gross profit: $19,782Only if all four targets are realized at their planned prices.Planned total gross loss: -$4,638If all ten contracts fill and the stop executes at its stated price.Blended reward-to-risk: 4.27:1A payoff ratio, not a success probability or expected return.

Trade management after the first profit target

The initial stop at $4,126.60 is $46.38 below the full-position average entry. If gold reaches TP1 at $4,257, I would consider reducing exposure and moving the remaining stop toward the actual weighted-average entry, subject to the filled orders and prevailing price structure. At TP2, protecting accumulated gains becomes increasingly important if a smaller runner remains.

Moving a stop toward entry does not guarantee a breakeven result. Gold futures can move rapidly, and execution prices, fees and gaps all affect outcomes.

What would strengthen or weaken this gold recovery?

Scenarios to watch

Recovery gaining credibility: Buyers defend the intended entriesHigher lows and a sustained move toward $4,257 and $4,338 would support an improving recovery, although the four-hour trend still needs confirmation.The trade thesis deteriorates: Selling continues through the buy areaFilling more lower entries could reflect weakening support. $4,126.60 is the planned trade stop even though it sits within the wider $4,100 to $4,160 region.The market rallies without us: Some buy orders never fillA missed entry is not a reason to chase price or assume that the original full-position calculations still apply.

Why patience matters for this multi-week gold trade

The targets require progressively greater improvement in the price structure, particularly the ambitious final runner at $4,648. Meanwhile, upcoming U.S. inflation figures could influence Treasury yields, the dollar and gold futures, producing further volatility before a sustainable recovery develops.

There are two distinct questions: Can gold stabilize sufficiently for a patient entry? And can it then recover far enough to reach the distant targets? The first does not establish the second.

For me, the attraction is the combination of selective entries, measured exposure and several opportunities to take profits, not a certainty that gold will revisit $4,648. I would rather miss the first leg of a rally than abandon the entry plan because price moves higher without me.

What I'm also watching:

while bullion is attempting to gain traction, Eamonn at investingLive.com highlighted that gold's move higher in Asia on the Russia-Ukraine energy truce narrative rests on very shaky support, especially with Kyiv reporting fresh infrastructure strikes within hours and the core macro focus remaining tied to crude prices ahead of Wednesday's US CPI.

From a technical standpoint, as Justin from investingLive.com noted, gold buyers eyeing a decisive $4,200 breakout still face major hurdles around $4,220 and $4,256, meaning upside momentum will need sustained order flow and a clear reclaim of overhead resistance to confirm a lasting recovery.

item.title: Macro pulse: US bank earnings could reveal the hidden cost of surging Treasury yields
item.description:
It's earnings season again and as is always the case, the big banks on Wall Street will be the ones to kick start proceedings starting tomorrow.

While much of the usual focus will be on whether the banks manage to beat earnings expectations, there is perhaps a more important story running in the background this time around. That being how the recent surge in Treasury yields is impacting the banking sector and, by extension, the broader US economy.

Now, higher interest rates and yields aren't necessarily a bad thing for banks to begin with. They can charge more interest on loans and that potentially means fatter margins to work with in trying to earn more money. However, there's also the other side of the equation to be mindful about.

Higher borrowing costs are also likely to weigh more on demand conditions, in particular demand for loans. Just think about businesses deciding to hold back on expansion plans or households putting off from taking up a new mortgage because financing has become too expensive.

As such, that will be one of the key things to watch in the earnings reports this week.

Besides that, banks will also have to face higher funding costs as they may need to offer better deposit rates to keep customers from moving their money elsewhere. So even if lending income improves, that doesn't automatically translate to better profit margins.

And then there's also the question of credit quality. If borrowers struggle to keep up with repayments, banks could start seeing more missed payments and potentially higher loan losses. Any clues pointing in this direction would offer another indication to markets that tighter financial conditions are starting to take a toll on businesses and/or households.

Now of course, none of this means that we're starting to see major problems emerge in the banking sector. However, they do offer markets a useful gauge on whether the impact of higher yields is starting to filter through to the real economy.

So, don't just pay attention to how much money the banks are making this week. It'll be worth paying just as much attention to signs on whether their customers are starting to feel the pinch.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chart of the day: Gold price eyes $4,200 breakout, but buyers still face two major hurdles
item.description:
Gold buyers are making another attempt to decisively get above the $4,200 level to start the new week. The precious metal touched a high of $4,217 earlier in Asia trading but is now trickling back lower to the figure level again, which has been a key point of contention since last week already.

The region around $4,200-20 has been causing quite a bit of frustration for buyers, so I wouldn't say that gold has convinced of any break to the upside just yet. Having said that, there are at least some encouraging signs for buyers since the end of last week.

Looking at the hourly chart, gold had managed to climb above both its 100-hour (red line) and 200-hour (blue line) moving averages on Friday and is sticking with that for now. That is a welcome development for buyers, especially after having struggled to build any real momentum in recent weeks. So, the price move here suggests that the near-term technical picture is at least looking more constructive. However, there is still some work to be done.

Despite the near-term bias siding with buyers now, they are still unable to really shake off the $4,200 level. Besides that, they have to also contend with swing region resistance closer to $4,220. That has been a stumbling block for any upside pushes so far this month, so getting past that would offer a stronger signal that buyers are attempting a stronger recovery.

But even then, the daily chart presents another challenge not too far away.

The 100-day moving average (red line) around $4,256 remains a key technical hurdle to any upside momentum. Unless buyers can also firmly break above that, I will be hesitant to suggest that the rebound in gold since the end of last week has much legs to run.

On the flip side though, another rejection around $4,200-20 could see sellers step back into the picture with more confidence. That will turn back the focus on the key hourly moving averages around $4,148-56 next before potentially eyeing the supportive region around $4,100-17 from the end September and early October lows.

For now, getting above $4,200 is the first step that buyers need to take to establish some footing. However, getting past $4,220 and $4,256 is where the real test begins.

item.title: Stock earnings pick of the week: Can TSMC keep the AI boom running as US CPI looms?
item.description:
Q3 earnings season in Wall Street will kick off in earnest this week, as the big banks will begin reporting their quarterly results starting tomorrow. While that will hog some of the spotlight in the stock market, the AI boom continues to be one of the more closely watched themes. As such, I would pick TSMC as the stock to pay attention to in terms of earnings releases in the days ahead.

The big question now among investors with regards to the AI boom is whether all the spending on chips and data centers can keep going.

So, TSMC might offer a better idea of that when they report their earnings on Thursday, 15 October. As a reminder, TSMC is one of the biggest chip manufacturers in the world and plays a crucial role in the AI supply chain. Nvidia might be the more familiar household name as they design powerful chips needed to run AI applications, but someone still has to manufacture them. And that is where TSMC comes in.

Analysts are expecting EPS of around $4.42 for its US-listed shares, with net profit projected to surge roughly 65% to NT$746.3 billion.

Now, TSMC has already enjoyed a rather impressive quarter. The firm reported record revenue of NT$1.49 trillion ($46.7 billion), which is up 50% from a year ago and beating market expectations of NT$1.46 trillion. But with expectations already running so high, I would argue that it is definitely a very tall order to impress investors further from this point. In other words, investors might be looking for more than just another record-breaking quarter to be satisfied.

As such, there will be watchful eyes on whether TSMC can keep this momentum up heading into 2027. What the firm says about AI chip demand and whether customers are still looking to ramp up orders might be more important than the headline numbers themselves.

But before we even get to TSMC's earnings this week, there is also the broader market picture to consider.

The US CPI report on Wednesday will arguably be the bigger key risk event for markets this week. And with Treasury yields staying elevated, another hot inflation reading could put further pressure on tech stocks - regardless of how well TSMC performs.

Taking that into account, I reckon an upbeat outlook from TSMC could still offer some reassurance that the AI boom has room to run. However, whether that will be enough to keep AI stocks rallying is another question altogether.

I mean, investors are already paying a hefty premium for AI-related stocks. So, they might not have that much appetite to keep paying such high prices if inflation worries and rising bond yields continue to weigh on broader market sentiment.
